To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
for typical large proteins (e.g. 10–150kD) in the rat, systemic bioavailability following inhalation is very low (˜≤ 1%) and that this does not appear to be a function of protein molecular weight.

for typical large proteins (˜10–150kDA), systemic bioavailability (BA), defined as the fraction of the inhaled dose that is absorbed into the systemic circulation, following inhalation exposure in the rat is low (˜≤ 1%).

for typical large proteins (˜10–150kDA), systemic bioavailability following inhalation exposure in rats is low (˜≤ 1%), that addition of a polyethylene glyco moiety on a large protein (˜150kDa) can decrease systemic bioavailability even further, and that direct effects on the lung, such as accumulation, should be considered when evaluating the hazard potential of proteins with lung targets.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the bioavailability and clearance of proteins following inhalation exposure in rats.
the development of a method for the determination of the bioavailability of protein therapeutic agents in the rat following intravenous or inhalation exposure.
the bioavailability of protein therapeutic drugs after inhalation exposure.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the bioavailability of protein therapies following inhalation is very low, at 1% or less, and therefore, a default 100‐fold safety factor for inhalation exposures is warranted when determining OELs for this class of compounds.
the systemic bioavailability of proteins after inhalation exposure is very low (˜≤ 1%), which is consistent with the default assumption of 1% BA used in OEL calculations.
the bioavailability of the proteins in this study after an inhalation of 10–150k Da proteins was low, at 0.1–1%.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
for typical protein therapeutics (10–150 kDa) with a lung‐specific target, a default ˜≤ 1% bioavailable assumption is reasonable to use when calculating OEL values.
for typical protein therapeutics, a default bioavailability factor of 1% is reasonable when calculating OEL values.
the inhalation exposure of large proteins (10 to 150kDa) in a manner mimics worker exposure results in very low systemic BA.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the bioavailability of inhaled proteins is very low and the direct effects in the lung should be assessed.
the default 1% bioassay factor should be applied to all proteins when calculating OEL values.
for typical protein therapeutics, systemic bioavailability after an inhalation dose is low, and a default bioavailability factor of 1% is appropriate when calculating OEL.
